findings.impact: The project could pass its release gates while reproducing the Node-only admission the owner rejected.
findings.text: The acceptance requirement for two-target sparse plans applies only to each demonstrably supported slice, but does not require any non-Node slice to be supported. Python and Go fixtures could always fall back to the full profile while only Node demonstrates selection, leaving the owner-requested multilingual impact capability unproven. Name a minimum supported set and require a real sparse case in at least one non-Node ecosystem, retaining conservative bounded/full fallback tests for unsupported constructs.

findings.impact: A failing Go test can be skipped while the report claims no uncertainty.
findings.text:
src/impact/go-static.ts:61-66 treats any README.md or LICENSE as irrelevant unless explicitly embedded, but Go automatically loads tracked fuzz corpus files under testdata/fuzz/<FuzzName>/ regardless of filename. In a two-package module with FuzzValue in a/fuzz_test.go, changing only a/testdata/fuzz/FuzzValue/README.md from 'go test fuzz v1
int(1)
' to 'go test fuzz v1
int(2)
' changes go test ./a from passing to failing. The impact CLI returns conditional with no gaps or fallback and omits a/fuzz_test.go. Model corpus-to-package test dependencies or conservatively fall back, including filenames normally classified as documentation.

findings.impact: The delivered architecture fails the approved multilingual shared-graph contract and cannot preserve import uncertainty and provenance for scope decisions.
findings.text: The approved multilingual design requires a shared Trail-code conservative fact pipeline preserving raw imports/re-exports, candidate provenance and combined reverse dependencies. src/impact/facts.ts:48-49 filters out import intents, and src/impact/analyze.ts:300-332 builds upstream graphs but uses a separate goClosure over the Go-specific parser when selecting Go changes. The upstream graph and its relations are therefore discarded for the supported Go path; this does not implement the requested common multilingual foundation or preserve raw import uncertainty. Connect the supported Go selection to shared conservative import facts and reverse relationships, preserving source/revision provenance and scoped or global uncertainty as required by the design.

findings.impact: Ordinary Go projects receive global fallback, undermining the required practical sparse behavior; the misleading gap impedes diagnosis.
findings.text: The Go model recognizes only testing and embed standard-library imports; an otherwise conventional two-package module containing 'import \"fmt\"' returns full fallback for an isolated change, with an unresolved fmt import and a misleading message about the Node/TypeScript ESM model. Support and identify standard-library dependencies under the declared Go toolchain context so routine conventional Go modules achieve the approved useful sparse selection, and make fallback reasons identify the actual Go boundary.

findings.impact: The demonstrated missed test and shared-graph regressions can pass acceptance undetected.
findings.text: The frozen conditional contract has no regression for implicit Go fuzz corpus resources. Add an end-to-end two-commit case whose real go test passes before a corpus edit and fails after it, including a README.md-named corpus file; assert the impacted owning tests or an explicit safe fallback. Add representative conventional Go standard-library import and shared cross-language/raw import provenance coverage required by the approved design, including Python and mixed-language fixtures.

output.summary: Prior material findings are resolved: Go fuzz testdata triggers full fallback, raw import candidates are retained, Go dependencies join the shared reverse graph, and the supported standard-library case is selective. Four focused contract tests pass with Go installed.
Real Go fuzz failure and multilingual fallback regressions are meaningful and appropriately measured.

spec: Implement conservative impact analysis directly in this Trail-code fork specified in docs/test-impact/design.md, sections 1–6, 8, 11–13 and delivery steps 1–2. Use upstream base ca20a67764e99531a1cf272eea8354e2c16f71d9 and define versioned impact contracts and exact explicit endpoints. Analyze both snapshots, preserve ambiguity and analysis gaps, traverse complete reverse dependencies without arbitrary limits, handle deletions, renames and rebinding, and isolate and validate conservative caches. Report justified fallback scopes instead of silently omitting uncertainty. Include meaningful tests for endpoint semantics, graph completeness, gaps, cache freshness and representative dependency cases. Preserve upstream licensing and document the pinned source. Do not implement a replacement parser or assume normal navigation output is conservative. The full design and its acceptance matrix are binding; resolve open distribution and interface choices through the workflow. Work directly in this fork for a future upstream pull request; no separate test-impact repository or Git subtree. Preserve the separate Unity plugin branch. Where the design refers to a separate fork and adapter distribution, adapt it to this unified repository. Owner scope clarification: Initial release requires explicit committed Git endpoints only, and must work across platforms and filesystems with ordinary Git repositories, without Btrfs, privileged operations, special mounts or subvolumes. Worktree target support is deferred; reject it clearly rather than silently substituting a commit. Use ordinary test-runner execution with a stable-input assumption and a practical target preflight; do not require proof of checkout immutability, mutation monitoring, filesystem snapshots, or isolated checkout. Adapt the original worktree-specific acceptance cases accordingly.
